thousand-years.text: Which dates mark the period of about a thousand years studied in this chapter?
thousand-years.explanation: The chapter traces changes in the subcontinent from about 700 to 1750, a span of roughly a thousand years.

thousand-years.text: When the thirteenth-century chronicler Minhaj-i-Siraj used the word Hindustan, what did he mean by it?
options: The whole subcontinent from Kashmir to Kanyakumari
Only the Deccan and the far south
Areas of Punjab, Haryana and the land between the Ganga and Yamuna
thousand-years.explanation: For Minhaj-i-Siraj, Hindustan meant the lands that formed the core of the Delhi Sultan's territory, not the whole subcontinent.

thousand-years.text: Which ruler used the word Hindustan in the early sixteenth century for the geography, animals and culture of the whole subcontinent?
thousand-years.explanation: Babur used Hindustan in a much wider sense than Minhaj-i-Siraj had done three centuries earlier.

thousand-years.text: The word Hindu was originally used by Persian speakers for which people?
options: People who lived east of the river Indus
thousand-years.explanation: The word first described a place and its people, those living east of the Indus. Its use as a name for a religion came later.

thousand-years.text: Al-Idrisi, who prepared a map of the Indian subcontinent in 1154, was a(n)
thousand-years.explanation: Al-Idrisi was an Arab geographer. His map of 1154 shows how the subcontinent looked to a traveller-scholar of that time.

thousand-years.text: What is a manuscript?
options: A book printed in large numbers on a machine
A handwritten document that scribes copied by hand
A message carved on a stone wall
A coin issued by a king
thousand-years.explanation: Manuscripts were written and copied by hand, so each copy could differ a little from the others.

thousand-years.text: What are inscriptions?
options: Writings carved on hard surfaces such as stone or metal
Letters written on paper by scribes
thousand-years.explanation: Inscriptions are engraved on stone, metal or similar material, and often record gifts or the deeds of rulers.

thousand-years.text: Abu'l Fazl, who wrote the Akbarnama, was a historian at the court of which ruler?
thousand-years.explanation: Abu'l Fazl served Akbar and wrote a detailed chronicle of his reign, the Akbarnama.

thousand-years.text: Ziauddin Barani, a historian of the Delhi Sultanate, wrote a chronicle called
thousand-years.explanation: Barani wrote the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, a Persian chronicle of the Delhi Sultans.

thousand-years.text: Amir Khusrau, who used the word Hind for the region, was a
options: Poet of the Delhi Sultanate period
thousand-years.explanation: Amir Khusrau was a well-known poet of the fourteenth century who wrote about the land he lived in.

thousand-years.text: Into which three periods did British historians divide Indian history?
thousand-years.explanation: They named the periods after the religion of the rulers, calling them Hindu, Muslim and British.

thousand-years.text: What is the main problem with dividing Indian history into Hindu, Muslim and British periods?
options: It begins the story too early
It uses the rulers' religion as the main feature and ignores the many other changes and the variety in society
thousand-years.explanation: Societies in all periods were diverse and changed in many ways, so naming a whole age after one religion hides this.

thousand-years.text: In the usual three-part division of history that historians use today, which period lies between the ancient and the modern?
thousand-years.explanation: Historians divide history into ancient, medieval and modern, with the medieval period in the middle.

thousand-years.text: Which pair of a group and its region is correct?
thousand-years.explanation: The Ahoms were a group who ruled in Assam. The other pairs join groups to regions where they were not based.

thousand-years.text: The Marathas are a group that rose to power in which region?
thousand-years.explanation: The Marathas rose in Maharashtra and became a major political power.

thousand-years.text: In this period the Rajputs became prominent as
options: Traders who sailed across the seas
Warrior clans, many of whom became rulers
thousand-years.explanation: Rajputs were known as warrior families, and many Rajput clans ruled kingdoms in different regions.

thousand-years.text: The Sikhs are a community that grew in which region?
thousand-years.explanation: The Sikh community grew in Punjab, where it became a distinct religious and political group.

thousand-years.text: Babur is known as the founder of which empire?
thousand-years.explanation: Babur came from Central Asia and began the Mughal rule in the subcontinent.

thousand-years.text: The Tughlaqs and Khaljis were rulers of which state?
thousand-years.explanation: Both dynasties ruled from Delhi as Sultans, so their state is called the Delhi Sultanate.

thousand-years.text: The Vijayanagara Empire was centred in which part of the subcontinent?
thousand-years.explanation: Vijayanagara was a great empire of the south, with its capital at Hampi.

thousand-years.text: Which statement best describes regions and empires in this period?
options: Large empires and many regional kingdoms existed side by side, and each region developed its own culture
One empire ruled the whole subcontinent for the entire thousand years
Empires left no mark on the regions they ruled
Regions had no separate languages or traditions
thousand-years.explanation: Empires such as the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals grew alongside regional kingdoms and cultures, so the picture was varied.

thousand-years.text: The bhakti tradition stressed
options: Loving devotion of a person to God
Only the study of old texts in secret
thousand-years.explanation: Bhakti saints taught that personal love and devotion to God mattered most.

thousand-years.text: Who are Sufis?
options: Muslim mystics who stress love and devotion to God
thousand-years.explanation: Sufis were Muslim mystics who looked for a close, loving bond with God.

thousand-years.text: Where and in which century did Islam emerge?
thousand-years.explanation: Islam began in the Arabian peninsula in the seventh century and later spread to the subcontinent.

thousand-years.text: Which feature did bhakti saints and Sufis broadly share?
options: Stress on love and devotion to God, which welcomed ordinary people
Insistence that only kings could worship
Rejection of all songs and poetry
Worship only in temples built by rulers
thousand-years.explanation: Both traditions stressed loving devotion, and their message reached people of many backgrounds.

thousand-years.text: Bhakti saints often composed their songs in
options: The languages that ordinary people spoke
thousand-years.explanation: By singing in everyday languages, the saints made their message easy for common people to follow.

thousand-years.text: Which new technology of this period changed the way battles were fought?
thousand-years.explanation: Firearms came into use in combat in this period and affected how armies fought.

thousand-years.text: The Chola kings ruled mainly over which region?
thousand-years.explanation: The Cholas were a southern dynasty whose heartland was in what is now Tamil Nadu.

thousand-years.text: Rohan reads that Minhaj-i-Siraj used Hindustan for parts of north India, while Babur used it for the whole subcontinent. What does this show?
options: The meaning of a word can change with time and with the person using it
One of the two writers made a mistake
The word was not used in Persian writing
thousand-years.explanation: The same word carried different meanings in the thirteenth and the sixteenth centuries, so historians must read words in their own time.

thousand-years.text: In the fifteenth century, Gurpreet's ancestors lifted water from a well using a wheel with a row of pots turned by bullocks. What is this device called?
thousand-years.explanation: A wheel with pots that lift water for fields is the Persian wheel, a farming technology of this period.

thousand-years.text: Kavya finds a stone slab with letters carved on it. It records a gift made by a king to a temple. Which kind of source is this?
thousand-years.explanation: Writing carved on stone or metal is an inscription.

thousand-years.text: A historian finds two hand-copied versions of the same old book in different libraries, and some lines do not match. What is the most likely reason?
options: The author wrote two different books with the same name
Both copies were printed by machine
Inscriptions were added to the paper
Scribes copied by hand and sometimes made small changes
thousand-years.explanation: Manuscripts were copied by hand, and with each copy small changes could creep in.

thousand-years.text: Nandini's family has served for generations as scribes and secretaries in the offices of rulers. To which group does her family most likely belong?
thousand-years.explanation: Kayasthas were a group known for working as scribes and administrators.

thousand-years.text: Imran's teacher says that Abu'l Fazl wrote a long account of Akbar's reign. What kind of source is this?
options: An inscription on a stone pillar
A chronicle written by a court historian
A coin of the Mughal mint
thousand-years.explanation: A detailed record of a ruler's reign written by a historian at his court is a chronicle.

thousand-years.text: Arjun's old school book calls the years from 1200 to 1750 the Muslim period. His teacher points out that the great Vijayanagara kingdom of the south also flourished then. What does this show?
options: Rulers' religion never mattered to anyone
Labelling a whole age by the rulers' religion is misleading
The dates in the book are wrong
thousand-years.explanation: Rulers of many kinds existed in the same years, so naming the age after one religion ignores this variety.

thousand-years.text: At a dargah, Shabnam listens to devotional songs about love for God. These songs are linked to which tradition?
thousand-years.explanation: Sufism is the tradition of Muslim mystics, and devotional singing is part of it.

thousand-years.text: Grandmother's dish uses chillies and potatoes. Her teacher says these became part of our food during which time?
options: In the period covered in this chapter, between about 700 and 1750
In the days of the Harappan cities
Before the time of the Mauryas
thousand-years.explanation: Potatoes, corn, chillies, tea and coffee became part of the food of the subcontinent during this thousand-year period.

thousand-years.text: A coin is found in a field. Which of these can historians most directly learn from it?
options: The name or picture of the ruler who issued it
thousand-years.explanation: Coins often carry the name, picture or date of the ruler, which makes them a direct source about rule.

thousand-years.text: A weaver's family in a village in the fourteenth century gets much more yarn for cloth after a new device spreads. Which device is likely?
thousand-years.explanation: The spinning wheel made it easier to produce yarn, and it came into use in this period.

thousand-years.text: A historian reads a Persian chronicle by Barani, an Arabic map by Al-Idrisi and a Sanskrit inscription. Why must historians of this period know several languages?
options: All sources were written in English
Only one language was used, but with different scripts
Languages do not matter to historians
Sources were written in languages such as Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit and Turkish
thousand-years.explanation: Sources of this thousand years come in many languages, so historians must read or rely on translations of many of them.

thousand-years.text: Meera arranges these by when they began, earliest first: Chola, Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara, Mughal. Which order is correct?
thousand-years.explanation: The Cholas rose first, the Delhi Sultanate began in 1206, Vijayanagara in the fourteenth century, and the Mughals in 1526.

thousand-years.text: Arun's teacher says this chapter covers the years 700 to 1750. How many years is that?
thousand-years.explanation: 1750 - 700 = 1050 years, which is about a thousand years.

thousand-years.text: Match the worker with the technology of this period. Which pair is correct?
thousand-years.explanation: Weavers needed yarn, which the spinning wheel produced. The Persian wheel was for farming and firearms were for combat.

thousand-years.text: Two chroniclers wrote different accounts of the same Sultan's reign. What should a historian do?
options: Accept the longer account without question
Ignore both and stop the study
Compare both accounts with other sources such as inscriptions and coins
thousand-years.explanation: Historians check one source against others, because every writer has a point of view.

thousand-years.text: Which of these is NOT a source that historians use to study this period?
thousand-years.explanation: Inscriptions, coins and manuscripts are sources from the period itself, while a film from 1950 is far too late.

thousand-years.text: Which of these is NOT among the foods and drinks that became part of our food in this period?
thousand-years.explanation: Wheat was grown long before 700. Potatoes, chillies and coffee were among the newer additions.

thousand-years.text: Which of these was NOT a social or political group that grew in this period?
thousand-years.explanation: The Harappans lived thousands of years earlier. The other three are groups of this period.

thousand-years.text: Which of these was NOT a technology of this period?
thousand-years.explanation: The steam engine came much later. The other three were in use during the thousand years.

thousand-years.text: Which statement about Hindustan is NOT correct?
options: It has always meant exactly the same area as the Republic of India
Minhaj-i-Siraj used it for parts of north India
Babur used it for the wider subcontinent
thousand-years.explanation: The word meant different things to different writers, so it was not always the same as present-day India.

thousand-years.text: Which statement about these thousand years is NOT correct?
options: New social and political groups appeared
Society, farming and technology stayed the same throughout
thousand-years.explanation: The chapter describes many changes in this period, so saying nothing changed is wrong.

thousand-years.text: Which of these is NOT true of Sufis?
options: They taught only rulers and turned away ordinary people
They used music and song in devotion
thousand-years.explanation: Sufis welcomed people of many backgrounds. They did not turn ordinary people away.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): The word Hindustan meant different things to different writers over time. Reason (R): Words can change their meaning as time passes and as different people use them.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: The changing use of words explains why Hindustan had more than one meaning.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): Historians no longer accept the Hindu, Muslim and British division of Indian history. Reason (R): That division uses only the rulers' religion and ignores the variety in society and the economy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: The division is rejected because it hides the diversity of each age.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): Different manuscripts of the same book can differ from one another. Reason (R): Scribes copied manuscripts by hand and sometimes made small changes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: Hand copying led to small changes, which is why copies differ.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): Bhakti stressed loving devotion to God. Reason (R): Sufis were Muslim mystics.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: Both statements are true, but the fact that Sufis were mystics does not explain the bhakti emphasis on devotion.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): Potatoes, corn and chillies became part of our food in this period. Reason (R): These crops were grown in the subcontinent since Harappan times.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: The first statement is true, but the crops were new in this period, so the reason is false.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): Coins cannot give historians any information about rulers. Reason (R): Coins often carry the name or picture of the ruler who issued them.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: A is false because coins do tell us about rulers. R is true.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): Hindustan today means exactly what it meant to Minhaj-i-Siraj. Reason (R): Minhaj-i-Siraj used Hindustan for parts of north India.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: A is false because the meaning changed. R is true.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): The Rajputs became prominent as warrior clans in this period. Reason (R): The Marathas rose to power in Maharashtra.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: Both statements are true, but they describe two different groups, so one does not explain the other.

thousand-years.text: Assertion (A): Historians use many kinds of sources to study these thousand years. Reason (R): Only chronicles written by court historians are accepted as proof.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
thousand-years.explanation: A is true because historians use inscriptions, coins, manuscripts and chronicles. R is false.

new-kings.text: From about which century did many new dynasties begin to emerge in different parts of the subcontinent?
new-kings.explanation: The chapter begins with new dynasties emerging from about the seventh century onwards.

new-kings.text: Who was a samanta?
options: A priest who composed praise poems for kings
A merchant who belonged to a trading guild
A craftsperson who made bronze images in a temple
A subordinate warrior chief or landlord who accepted a king as his overlord
new-kings.explanation: Samantas were warrior chiefs and big landlords whom kings accepted as their subordinates.

new-kings.text: Devaraj was a warrior chief in the 8th century. At first he brought gifts to a great king every year and sent soldiers to help him. As Devaraj grew richer and stronger, he began to call himself a maha-samanta. What did this show?
options: He had been made a priest by the king
He had lost all his land to the king
He was claiming greater power and status and might even act independently
He had become the leader of a merchants' guild
new-kings.explanation: Samantas who gained wealth and power took grand titles like maha-samanta and sometimes asserted independence.

new-kings.text: Which of these was NOT expected of a samanta by his overlord?
options: To bring tribute and gifts for the king
To appoint the ministers of the king's court
To provide the king with military support
new-kings.explanation: Samantas brought gifts, attended the court and gave military help; they did not choose the king's ministers.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): Samantas never tried to become independent of their overlords. Reason (R): Samantas had to bring tribute and provide military support to their overlords.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: Samantas did owe tribute and soldiers (R is true), but as they grew strong some asserted independence, so A is false.

new-kings.text: Dantidurga was a chief of which dynasty?
new-kings.explanation: Dantidurga was a Rashtrakuta chief who rose against his overlord.

new-kings.text: The Rashtrakutas were at first subordinates of the Chalukyas of which region?
new-kings.explanation: The Rashtrakutas served the Chalukyas of Karnataka until Dantidurga overthrew his overlord.

new-kings.text: Aisha is arranging events on a timeline. Dantidurga overthrew his Chalukya overlord and made the Rashtrakutas independent. In which period should she place this event?
new-kings.explanation: The chapter places Dantidurga's rise in the middle of the eighth century.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): Dantidurga overthrew his Chalukya overlord. Reason (R): Dantidurga was a samanta of the Palas.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: Dantidurga was a Rashtrakuta chief serving the Chalukyas, not the Palas, so R is false.

new-kings.text: What does 'hiranyagarbha' literally mean?
new-kings.explanation: Hiranyagarbha means 'golden womb', the name of a ritual.

new-kings.text: Ravi has become a powerful chief but is not a Kshatriya by birth. He wants to be accepted as one, so he performs the hiranyagarbha ritual with the help of Brahmanas. What was this ritual believed to do?
options: Free his land from all tax
Lead to his rebirth as a Kshatriya
new-kings.explanation: When performed with Brahmanas' help, the ritual was thought to cause the performer's rebirth as a Kshatriya.

new-kings.text: Which grand title meaning 'great king, overlord of kings' was taken by new rulers?
new-kings.explanation: Rulers took titles like maha-raja-adhiraja to show they stood above other kings.

new-kings.text: The title 'tri-bhuvana-chakravartin' taken by some rulers means:
new-kings.explanation: Tri-bhuvana-chakravartin means lord of the three worlds.

new-kings.text: Surya is the treasurer of a king in the 9th century. Each year grain and coins come in from peasants, traders and craftspersons. According to the chapter, what was such revenue used for?
options: Only to buy jewels for the royal family
To return it to the farmers as gifts
To pay tribute to the rulers of Ghazni
To pay for the army, officials, temples and forts
new-kings.explanation: Revenue from producers paid for the king's army and officials and for building temples and forts.

new-kings.text: Which of these is NOT a title taken by new kings or powerful chiefs?
new-kings.explanation: Maha-mandaleshvara, maha-samanta and tri-bhuvana-chakravartin were titles of these times; Peshwa was not.

new-kings.text: Kannauj, over which three dynasties fought, lay in the valley of which river?
new-kings.explanation: The struggle was for control of Kannauj in the Ganga valley.

new-kings.text: Rukmini studies a map. A Pala kingdom, a Rashtrakuta kingdom and a Gurjara-Pratihara kingdom all sent their armies again and again to capture one city. Which city was it?
new-kings.explanation: The Palas, Rashtrakutas and Gurjara-Pratiharas fought over Kannauj.

new-kings.text: The Palas ruled over which region?
new-kings.explanation: The Palas were the dynasty of Bengal and Bihar.

new-kings.text: Which of these dynasties did NOT take part in the tripartite struggle for Kannauj?
new-kings.explanation: The struggle was among the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, not the Cholas.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): The fight over Kannauj is called a tripartite struggle. Reason (R): Three major dynasties took part in it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: 'Tripartite' means three-sided, and three dynasties fought for Kannauj.

new-kings.text: Which chief of the old Chola family of Uraiyur captured the Kaveri delta from the Muttaraiyar?
new-kings.explanation: Vijayalaya captured the delta and began the rise of the Cholas.

new-kings.text: Which town did Vijayalaya build in the Kaveri delta?
new-kings.explanation: Vijayalaya built the town of Thanjavur; Gangaikondacholapuram came later under Rajendra I.

new-kings.text: Vijayalaya built a temple at Thanjavur for which goddess?
new-kings.explanation: The temple built by Vijayalaya at Thanjavur was for the goddess Nishumbhasudini.

new-kings.text: In which year did Rajaraja I become king of the Cholas?
new-kings.explanation: Rajaraja I became king in 985 and began expanding Chola power.

new-kings.text: Which Chola ruler built the new capital Gangaikondacholapuram?
new-kings.explanation: Rajendra I, son of Rajaraja I, created the capital Gangaikondacholapuram.

new-kings.text: What does the name 'Gangaikondacholapuram' mean?
options: The town of the goddess of the Ganga
The Chola port on the Ganga
The town of the Chola who conquered the Ganga
The temple of the thousand lamps
new-kings.explanation: The name means the town of the Chola who took the Ganga, after Rajendra I's northern success.

new-kings.text: For a project, Kavya lists three places from the Chola story: Uraiyur (old home of the Chola family), Thanjavur (town built by Vijayalaya) and Gangaikondacholapuram (capital created by Rajendra I). Which order shows when they became important?
new-kings.explanation: The Cholas began at Uraiyur, Vijayalaya built Thanjavur, and Rajendra I later made Gangaikondacholapuram.

new-kings.text: Latha's class studies a Chola record. It says a group of villages was joined into one unit with its own council. What was such a unit called?
new-kings.explanation: In the Chola kingdom, villages were grouped into units called nadu.

new-kings.text: Which Chola local body was an assembly of Brahmana landowners?
new-kings.explanation: The sabha was the assembly of landowning Brahmanas in brahmadeya villages.

new-kings.text: Which Chola term means an organisation of merchants?
new-kings.explanation: The nagaram was the body of merchants in Chola towns.

new-kings.text: Anbu lives in a Chola village. He says, 'Our ur meets under the banyan tree.' What was an ur?
new-kings.explanation: The ur was the assembly of a village.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): All Chola local bodies were open only to Brahmanas. Reason (R): The nagaram was an organisation of merchants.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: The nagaram was made up of merchants, so not every local body was only for Brahmanas; R is true and A is false.

new-kings.text: Which of these is NOT connected with Chola local administration?
new-kings.explanation: Hiranyagarbha is a ritual, while sabha, ur and nagaram were local bodies.

new-kings.text: Which Chola king built the great temple at Thanjavur?
new-kings.explanation: Rajaraja I built the great temple at Thanjavur.

new-kings.text: The great Shiva temple built by Rajaraja I at Thanjavur was completed in:
new-kings.explanation: The Thanjavur temple of Rajaraja I was completed in 1010.

new-kings.text: On a school trip to Thanjavur, Anil sees a huge Shiva temple with a tall tower. His guide says it was named after the king who built it, Rajaraja. What is its other common name?
new-kings.explanation: The Rajarajeshvara temple at Thanjavur is also called the Brihadeshvara temple.

new-kings.text: Why did Chola kings build grand temples like the one at Thanjavur?
options: Only to hold meetings of the sabha
To show their devotion as well as their power and wealth
Only to store weapons for wars
To stop the Kaveri from flooding
new-kings.explanation: Kings built great temples to show devotion and to display their power and wealth.

new-kings.text: Which Chola art is considered among the finest in the world?
new-kings.explanation: Chola bronze images are famous as some of the finest in the world.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): Temples were centres of economic life in Chola times, not only of worship. Reason (R): Temples received land and gifts and gave work to many craftspersons and others.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: Because temples held land and wealth and employed many people, they were centres of the economy too.

new-kings.text: Kamal's family farms in the heart of the Chola kingdom, on the fertile delta of a river. Which river is it?
new-kings.explanation: The Chola heartland was the delta of the Kaveri river.

new-kings.text: Pallichchhandam was land gifted to:
new-kings.explanation: Pallichchhandam was land given to Jaina institutions.

new-kings.text: A Chola village sets aside a piece of land to support the upkeep of a school. What was such land called?
new-kings.explanation: Land given for the maintenance of a school was called shalabhoga.

new-kings.text: Vellanvagai was the name for the land of:
new-kings.explanation: Vellanvagai was land owned by non-Brahmana peasants.

new-kings.text: Pushpa's village in Chola Tamil Nadu gets little river water in the dry months. How did people bring water to their fields?
options: By digging wells and building tanks
By bringing canals from the Ganga
By drawing water from the sea
new-kings.explanation: Wells and tanks helped bring water to fields in Chola times.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): Devadana land was gifted to temples. Reason (R): Vellanvagai was the land of non-Brahmana peasant owners.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: Both statements are true but they are separate facts about different kinds of land, so R does not explain A.

new-kings.text: What is a prashasti?
options: A piece in praise of a ruler, often put into inscriptions
new-kings.explanation: A prashasti praises a ruler and his achievements.

new-kings.text: Nandini finds an old inscription calling a king 'conqueror of the whole earth', but other records show he lost many battles. What should she keep in mind?
options: The king must have conquered every country
Every line of the inscription must be false
Inscriptions are never useful to historians
Prashastis praise rulers and may exaggerate, so she should check other sources
new-kings.explanation: Prashastis are in praise of rulers and not always literally true, so historians cross-check them.

new-kings.text: Which of these is NOT true about prashastis?
options: They praise the achievements of rulers
They may not always be literally true
They were written to criticise rulers
new-kings.explanation: Prashastis were meant to praise, not to criticise.

new-kings.text: Where do historians commonly find prashastis?
options: In inscriptions engraved on stone or metal
In school notebooks of the time
new-kings.explanation: Prashastis are found in inscriptions engraved on stone or copper plates.

new-kings.text: Prithviraj Chauhan belonged to which dynasty?
new-kings.explanation: Prithviraj Chauhan was a ruler of the Chahamana (Chauhan) family.

new-kings.text: Prithviraj III defeated an Afghan ruler in 1191 but lost to him in the next battle in 1192. Who was this ruler?
new-kings.explanation: Prithviraj III beat Sultan Muhammad Ghori in 1191 but lost to him in 1192.

new-kings.text: Neha visits Ajmer fort and learns about Prithviraj Chauhan, a Chahamana king. Around which places did the Chahamanas rule?
new-kings.explanation: The Chahamanas ruled the region around Delhi and Ajmer.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): The Chahamanas are later known as the Chauhans. Reason (R): Prithviraj III belonged to the Chahamana family.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: Both are true, but the second is a separate fact and does not explain the change of name.

new-kings.text: Rafiq reads about a sultan named Mahmud who ruled from the town of Ghazni. In which present-day country is Ghazni?
new-kings.explanation: Ghazni is in Afghanistan.

new-kings.text: Anwar reads that a sultan from Afghanistan attacked a famous, wealthy temple in Gujarat and carried away its treasures. Which temple was it?
new-kings.explanation: Mahmud of Ghazni raided the wealthy Somnath temple in Gujarat.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): Mahmud of Ghazni raided the subcontinent almost every year. Reason (R): He wanted the wealth of rich temples to build up his capital at Ghazni.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: Mahmud's raids targeted wealthy temples, and much of the loot was used to make Ghazni a splendid capital.

new-kings.text: Which of these is NOT true of Mahmud of Ghazni?
options: He raided wealthy temples such as Somnath
He used the wealth he carried away to make Ghazni a splendid capital
He built the Brihadeshvara temple at Thanjavur
new-kings.explanation: The Thanjavur temple was built by Rajaraja I, a Chola, not by Mahmud.

new-kings.text: Al-Biruni wrote a famous book on the subcontinent called:
new-kings.explanation: Al-Biruni's Arabic book on the subcontinent is the Kitab-ul-Hind.

new-kings.text: Assertion (A): Al-Biruni wrote the Kitab-ul-Hind about the subcontinent. Reason (R): Al-Biruni was a court scholar of the Chola king Rajaraja I.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
new-kings.explanation: He did write the Kitab-ul-Hind, but he was not a Chola scholar; he came to the subcontinent with Mahmud of Ghazni's time.

new-kings.text: Which of these is NOT true of Al-Biruni?
options: He fought for Prithviraj Chauhan against Muhammad Ghori
His writings are an important source on the subcontinent of his time
new-kings.explanation: Al-Biruni was a scholar and writer, not a soldier in Prithviraj Chauhan's army.

delhi-sultans.text: Which Rajput dynasty first made Delhi the capital of a kingdom?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Delhi first became the capital of a kingdom under the Tomara Rajputs, before the Chauhans took it over.

delhi-sultans.text: In the middle of the twelfth century the Tomaras of Delhi were defeated by which rulers?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Chauhans of Ajmer defeated the Tomaras and Delhi came under their rule.

delhi-sultans.text: In which year did the Delhi Sultanate begin?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Delhi Sultanate began in 1206, when Qutbuddin Aibak became its first ruler.

delhi-sultans.text: Who was the first ruler of the Mamluk (Slave) dynasty?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Qutbuddin Aibak ruled from 1206 and started the Mamluk dynasty.

delhi-sultans.text: Which ruler of the Mamluk dynasty ruled from 1266 to 1287?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Balban ruled Delhi from 1266 to 1287, late in the Mamluk dynasty.

delhi-sultans.text: Raziya Sultan was the daughter of which Sultan?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Raziya was Iltutmish's daughter and became Sultan after him in 1236.

delhi-sultans.text: Which Sultan introduced token currency, using cheaper metal coins in place of silver ones?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Muhammad Tughluq tried token coins, but the plan did not work well.

delhi-sultans.text: Muhammad Tughluq shifted his capital from Delhi to which place?
delhi-sultans.explanation: He moved the capital to Daulatabad in the Deccan, a decision that became famous in history.

delhi-sultans.text: The Qutb Minar stands in which part of the country?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Qutb Minar is in the Mehrauli area of Delhi.

delhi-sultans.text: Which dynasty ruled Delhi from 1290 to 1320?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Khalji dynasty held the throne of Delhi from 1290 to 1320.

delhi-sultans.text: The chronicles written about the Delhi Sultans were mostly in which language?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Court historians of the Sultanate wrote their chronicles (tawarikh) in Persian.

delhi-sultans.text: Who founded the Khalji dynasty in 1290?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Jalaluddin Khalji started the dynasty, and his successor Alauddin Khalji later became its best-known ruler.

delhi-sultans.text: What was the name of the silver coin of the Delhi Sultans?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Sultans issued the silver tanka, while the jital was a copper coin.

delhi-sultans.text: In which year did Raziya become the Sultan of Delhi?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Raziya succeeded her father Iltutmish in 1236.

delhi-sultans.text: Which general of Alauddin Khalji led armies into south India?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Malik Kafur, a trusted general of Alauddin Khalji, led campaigns in the south.

delhi-sultans.text: Which Sultan fixed the prices of goods in the markets of Delhi?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Alauddin Khalji controlled market prices so that his soldiers could live on their cash pay.

delhi-sultans.text: Who founded the Tughluq dynasty in 1320?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Ghiyasuddin Tughluq started the Tughluq dynasty, which ruled until 1414.

delhi-sultans.text: Which was the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Lodis ruled from 1451 and their rule ended in 1526.

delhi-sultans.text: Which dynasty came to power in Delhi right after the Tughluqs?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Sayyids ruled from 1414 to 1451, after the Tughluqs.

delhi-sultans.text: In which year did Muhammad Ghori defeat Prithviraj Chauhan, opening the way for Turkish rule in Delhi?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Prithviraj Chauhan lost to Muhammad Ghori in 1192, and the Chauhan rule ended.

delhi-sultans.text: Before he became the first Sultan, what position did Qutbuddin Aibak hold?
options: A slave general of Muhammad Ghori
A minister of the Tomara kings
A prince of the Chauhan family
delhi-sultans.explanation: Aibak rose as a slave general of Muhammad Ghori and then founded his own rule in Delhi.

delhi-sultans.text: Who became the ruler of Delhi after Muhammad Tughluq died in 1351?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Firuz Shah Tughluq came to the throne in 1351 after Muhammad Tughluq.

delhi-sultans.text: Why was Raziya removed from the throne in 1240?
options: Her army lost to Muhammad Ghori at Tarain
She shifted the capital to Daulatabad
Many nobles were unhappy at a woman trying to rule independently
She gave up the throne to join the Mongols
delhi-sultans.explanation: Raziya was an able ruler, but many powerful nobles were unhappy at her attempts to rule independently and did not like being ruled by a woman.

delhi-sultans.text: Before Muhammad Tughluq renamed it Daulatabad, the town was known as what?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Daulatabad was the older town of Devagiri in the Deccan.

delhi-sultans.text: Which book by Ziyauddin Barani is a chronicle of the Delhi Sultans?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Barani wrote the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi in Persian, while Tabaqat-i-Nasiri was by Minhaj-i-Siraj.

delhi-sultans.text: Alauddin Khalji ruled Delhi from 1296 until which year?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Alauddin Khalji's reign ran from 1296 to 1316.

delhi-sultans.text: Which people from Central Asia attacked north India during the days of the Delhi Sultans?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Mongols came from Central Asia and raided the Sultanate, especially in Alauddin Khalji's time.

delhi-sultans.text: To guard the Sultanate against Mongol raids, Alauddin Khalji built up what kind of force?
options: A fleet of ships on the Indus
A force made only of elephants
A large standing army paid in cash
delhi-sultans.explanation: Alauddin raised a large standing army and paid its soldiers in cash, which is why he also controlled prices.

delhi-sultans.text: Meera is visiting a museum in Delhi. She sees old coins called dehliwal and reads that they travelled widely in trade. In which period were these coins minted?
options: When Delhi had become a capital and a busy trading centre under the Tomaras and Chauhans
Only under Muhammad Tughluq's token currency
Before any king ruled from Delhi
delhi-sultans.explanation: Dehliwal coins were minted when Delhi grew into a capital and commercial centre under the Tomaras and Chauhans.

delhi-sultans.text: Aman is a muqti in the Sultanate. The Sultan has given him an iqta, a territory to look after. What is Aman expected to do?
options: Write chronicles in Persian for the court
Collect revenue from the iqta and keep soldiers ready for the Sultan
Mint tanka coins and sell them to the public
Hand the iqta to his sons when he dies
delhi-sultans.explanation: A muqti collected revenue from his iqta and kept soldiers for the Sultan's army.

delhi-sultans.text: Farida reads that a woman ruled Delhi in 1236, that she was the daughter of Iltutmish, and that Minhaj-i-Siraj praised her as more able than her brothers. Which ruler is this?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Raziya, daughter of Iltutmish, was Sultan of Delhi from 1236 to 1240.

delhi-sultans.text: In 1300 a shopkeeper in Delhi, Lakshmi, finds that grain and cloth must be sold at prices fixed by the Sultan. Why did the Sultan do this?
options: So that foreign traders would stop coming to Delhi
So that coins could be changed from silver to copper
So that the Qutb Minar could be completed sooner
So that soldiers paid in cash could buy what they needed cheaply and he could keep a big army
delhi-sultans.explanation: By fixing low prices, Alauddin Khalji made his soldiers' cash pay go further, so he could afford a large army.

delhi-sultans.text: Sohan is paid in copper token coins that are meant to have the value of silver tankas. He does not trust them, so he keeps his old silver coins and uses the tokens only to pay his taxes. What does this show about Muhammad Tughluq's token currency?
options: The scheme failed because people did not trust the tokens
The scheme succeeded because everyone trusted it
The scheme was stopped by the Mongols
The scheme made the tanka a copper coin forever
delhi-sultans.explanation: When people did not trust the cheap tokens and kept their gold and silver, the token currency failed.

delhi-sultans.text: A teacher shows a map marking Delhi, Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai, and says Khalji armies marched to all of them. What does this show?
options: The Sultanate never went beyond Delhi
The Sultanate's power reached beyond north India into the Deccan and the far south
The Sultanate was confined to Ajmer
The Sultans only fought Mongols in Central Asia
delhi-sultans.explanation: Alauddin Khalji's armies under Malik Kafur pushed into the Deccan and the south.

delhi-sultans.text: Kabir's grandfather tells him a story about a famous battle at Tarain in 1192, in which Muhammad Ghori defeated a Chauhan king of Ajmer. Who was the king?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Prithviraj Chauhan lost to Muhammad Ghori in 1192.

delhi-sultans.text: Kavya is studying Raziya. She finds a chronicler who lived in her time and judged her more able and qualified than all her brothers. Who is this chronicler?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Minhaj-i-Siraj, author of Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, praised Raziya's ability.

delhi-sultans.text: Ananya's timeline card says: ruled 1210-1236, and his daughter ruled after him. Which Sultan is this?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Iltutmish ruled from 1210 to 1236 and was followed by his daughter Raziya.

delhi-sultans.text: Tanvi's family were Jain merchants in Delhi in the twelfth century and built temples there. Why was Delhi good for them?
options: It was the only port on the coast
It had become a capital and an important place of trade
The Mongols had made it their market
It was the capital of the Lodis
delhi-sultans.explanation: Delhi became a capital and a commercial centre, which drew rich merchants to it.

delhi-sultans.text: Muqti Rahman was moved from one iqta to another after a few years. Why did the Sultan transfer muqtis?
options: Because every muqti had to learn to mint coins
Because iqtas could only be given to Mongol soldiers
Iqtas were not hereditary and the Sultan did not want muqtis to become too powerful
Because the muqtis wanted to shift the capital
delhi-sultans.explanation: Iqtas were not passed on to sons, and transfers kept muqtis under the Sultan's control.

delhi-sultans.text: Sunita buys vegetables in Delhi's market with a small copper coin of the Sultans. What was this copper coin called?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The copper coin of the Sultanate was the jital, while the silver one was the tanka.

delhi-sultans.text: Dev arranges five cards: Khalji, Lodi, Mamluk, Tughluq, Sayyid. In which order did these dynasties rule Delhi?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The order is Mamluk (1206), Khalji (1290), Tughluq (1320), Sayyid (1414), Lodi (1451).

delhi-sultans.text: Latika notes that most chronicles of the Sultans were written by secretaries and scholars close to the court. What should she do when using them?
options: Trust every word since they are in Persian
Compare them with other sources, because they often show the court's own view
Ignore them since they were not about the Sultans
Treat them as written by the Mongols
delhi-sultans.explanation: Court writers tended to praise their patrons, so historians compare chronicles with other evidence.

delhi-sultans.text: Riya reads a board at Mehrauli: 'This tower was begun by the first Sultan and completed by a later Sultan of the same dynasty.' Which two rulers are meant?
options: Alauddin Khalji began it and Balban completed it
Iltutmish began it and Raziya completed it
Qutbuddin Aibak began it and Iltutmish completed it
Muhammad Tughluq began it and Firuz Shah completed it
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Qutb Minar was started by Qutbuddin Aibak and finished by Iltutmish.

delhi-sultans.text: Naina's book says the first dynasty of the Sultanate was called Mamluk. What does this tell us about it?
options: Its rulers came from the Tomara family
Its rulers were all Mongol chiefs
Its early rulers had begun as slave soldiers who rose to power
delhi-sultans.explanation: Mamluk means a slave, and the Slave dynasty began with a former slave general, Qutbuddin Aibak.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): Alauddin Khalji could keep a very large army. Reason (R): He fixed low prices in the markets so that cash salaries of soldiers went a long way.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: Low controlled prices let his soldiers manage on their pay, so the big army was affordable.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): Muhammad Tughluq's token currency was a failure. Reason (R): People did not trust the token coins and kept their gold and silver.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: Because people did not trust the cheap tokens, the scheme lost its value, which explains why it failed.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): Muqtis were moved from one iqta to another from time to time. Reason (R): Iqtas were hereditary and always passed on to the muqti's sons.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: A is true, but iqtas were not hereditary, so R is false.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): Raziya was a Sultan of Delhi. Reason (R): She was the daughter of Balban.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: Raziya was Sultan, but she was the daughter of Iltutmish, not Balban.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): The Delhi Sultanate was founded in 1206 by Prithviraj Chauhan. Reason (R): Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated by Muhammad Ghori in 1192.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Sultanate began under Qutbuddin Aibak in 1206, so A is false, while R is a true fact.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): The Mamluk dynasty is also called the Slave dynasty. Reason (R): Its first ruler, Qutbuddin Aibak, had started out as a slave general.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: The name comes from the slave origins of its founder, so R explains A.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): The Qutb Minar stands at Mehrauli in Delhi. Reason (R): The Tughluq dynasty ruled from 1320 to 1414.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: Both statements are true, but the Tughluq dates have nothing to do with where the Qutb Minar stands.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): Malik Kafur led armies to south India. Reason (R): Alauddin Khalji ruled before Ghiyasuddin Tughluq.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: Both are true, but the order of the two rulers does not explain Malik Kafur's campaigns.

delhi-sultans.text: Assertion (A): Daulatabad, the capital Muhammad Tughluq shifted to, lay in the far north of India. Reason (R): Daulatabad was earlier known as Devagiri.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
delhi-sultans.explanation: Daulatabad was in the Deccan, so A is false, while R is true.

delhi-sultans.text: Which of these is NOT a dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Guptas ruled long before the Sultanate, while the other three were Sultanate dynasties.

delhi-sultans.text: Which of these rulers is NOT from the Mamluk (Slave) dynasty?
delhi-sultans.explanation: Alauddin Khalji belonged to the Khalji dynasty, not the Mamluk dynasty.

delhi-sultans.text: Which of these is NOT true of Muhammad Tughluq?
options: He moved the capital to Daulatabad
He founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Sultanate began in 1206 under Qutbuddin Aibak, long before Muhammad Tughluq.

delhi-sultans.text: Which of these is NOT a feature of the iqta system?
options: The muqti kept soldiers for the Sultan
Muqtis were transferred from time to time
The muqti's sons inherited the iqta
delhi-sultans.explanation: Iqtas were not hereditary, so sons did not inherit them.

delhi-sultans.text: Which of these is NOT a coin of the Delhi Sultanate period?
delhi-sultans.explanation: The guinea was an English coin, while the others were coins used in the time of the Delhi Sultans.

delhi-sultans.text: Which of these statements about Raziya is NOT correct?
options: She ruled Delhi for twenty-five years
Minhaj-i-Siraj thought she was more able than her brothers
delhi-sultans.explanation: Raziya ruled only from 1236 to 1240, which is about four years.

delhi-sultans.text: Which of these statements about the Qutb Minar is NOT correct?
options: It was begun by Muhammad Tughluq
delhi-sultans.explanation: The Qutb Minar was begun by Qutbuddin Aibak, long before Muhammad Tughluq.

mughal-empire.text: The name 'Mughal' is a variation of the name of which people?
mughal-empire.explanation: Mughal comes from Mongol, because the dynasty was proud of its link to the Mongol ruler Genghis Khan.

mughal-empire.text: From their mother's side, the Mughals were descended from which Mongol ruler?
mughal-empire.explanation: The Mughals traced their mother's line to Genghis Khan, the great Mongol ruler.

mughal-empire.text: Which ruler, an ancestor of the Mughals on their father's side, captured Delhi in 1398?
mughal-empire.explanation: Timur, the ruler of Central Asia, captured Delhi in 1398, and the Mughals were proud of being his descendants.

mughal-empire.text: Who founded the Mughal Empire in India?
mughal-empire.explanation: Babur came from Central Asia and began Mughal rule in India after winning at Panipat in 1526.

mughal-empire.text: Which ruler did Babur defeat at the First Battle of Panipat?
mughal-empire.explanation: Babur defeated the Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.

mughal-empire.text: Which Mughal emperor was defeated by Sher Khan and had to flee to Iran for some years?
mughal-empire.explanation: Sher Khan defeated Humayun at Chausa in 1539 and at Kanauj in 1540, and Humayun left for Iran.

mughal-empire.text: Sher Shah Suri introduced a silver coin that later Mughal rulers also used. What was it called?
mughal-empire.explanation: Sher Shah issued a silver coin called the rupya, and the name survives today as the rupee.

mughal-empire.text: In which year did Humayun regain his throne after defeating the Sur rulers?
mughal-empire.explanation: Humayun returned from Iran and won back Delhi in 1555, but he died the next year.

mughal-empire.text: In 1556, whom did Akbar's army defeat in the Second Battle of Panipat?
mughal-empire.explanation: The Second Battle of Panipat in 1556 was won by Akbar's side against Hemu.

mughal-empire.text: Which pair of regions was brought under Mughal rule during Akbar's campaigns of expansion?
mughal-empire.explanation: Akbar's armies extended Mughal rule over regions such as Gujarat and Bengal.

mughal-empire.text: Who wrote the Akbarnama?
mughal-empire.explanation: Abu'l Fazl was Akbar's friend and court historian, and he wrote the Akbarnama.

mughal-empire.text: Which book forms the third part of the Akbarnama?
mughal-empire.explanation: The Akbarnama has three books, and the third one is the Ain-i-Akbari.

mughal-empire.text: What does the term 'sulh-i-kul' mean?
mughal-empire.explanation: Sulh-i-kul means universal peace, the idea of treating people of all faiths fairly.

mughal-empire.text: Akbar was the son of which Mughal ruler?
mughal-empire.explanation: Humayun, who regained Delhi in 1555, was the father of Akbar. Babur was Humayun's father.

mughal-empire.text: Nur Jahan was the wife of which Mughal emperor?
mughal-empire.explanation: Nur Jahan was the powerful wife of the emperor Jahangir.

mughal-empire.text: Which monument at Agra did Shah Jahan build in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal?
mughal-empire.explanation: The Taj Mahal was built by Shah Jahan in memory of Mumtaz Mahal.

mughal-empire.text: In which year did Aurangzeb die?
mughal-empire.explanation: Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 and died in 1707.

mughal-empire.text: According to the Mughal tradition of inheritance, how was a ruler's property meant to be shared?
options: By a vote of the common people
mughal-empire.explanation: The Mughals did not follow the rule that only the eldest son inherits; every son had a claim to a share.

mughal-empire.text: The word 'mansab' means:
mughal-empire.explanation: Mansab is a Persian word for rank or position, and an official who held one was a mansabdar.

mughal-empire.text: In the mansabdari system, what did 'zat' show?
options: The number of horsemen he had to keep
His age at joining the service
The personal rank and salary of the mansabdar
mughal-empire.explanation: Zat showed a mansabdar's personal status in the imperial order and decided his salary.

mughal-empire.text: What was a 'jagir' in the Mughal system?
options: Land whose revenue was assigned to a mansabdar in place of a salary
A tax paid only by merchants
A cash gift from the royal treasury
A school run by the emperor
mughal-empire.explanation: A jagir was a revenue assignment: the mansabdar received the income from the land rather than owning it.

mughal-empire.text: Which revenue officer of Akbar carried out a careful survey of crop yields and prices before the zabt system was set up?
mughal-empire.explanation: Todar Mal studied crop yields, prices and cultivated area, and his survey formed the base of the zabt system.

mughal-empire.text: Who were zamindars in the Mughal period?
options: Officers sent from Delhi who were transferred every few years
Merchants who sold goods at ports
Local headmen or chiefs who held power in the countryside and helped collect revenue
Judges who sat in the royal court
mughal-empire.explanation: Zamindars were local landholders and chiefs, and the Mughals depended on them to collect revenue from peasants.

mughal-empire.text: Which Rajput clan of Mewar refused to accept Akbar's authority for many years?
mughal-empire.explanation: The Sisodiya Rajputs of Mewar, under Rana Udai Singh, did not submit to Akbar, and Chittor was besieged in 1568.

mughal-empire.text: In 1527, Babur defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar in which battle?
mughal-empire.explanation: Babur won the Battle of Khanwa in 1527 against the Rajput ruler Rana Sanga.

mughal-empire.text: Which two Deccan kingdoms were conquered by Aurangzeb?
mughal-empire.explanation: Aurangzeb spent long years in the Deccan and brought Bijapur and Golconda under Mughal control.

mughal-empire.text: Which Persian ruler invaded Delhi in 1739 and carried away great treasures?
mughal-empire.explanation: Nadir Shah attacked Delhi in 1739, which showed how weak the later Mughal emperors had become.

mughal-empire.text: Under the zabt system, how was the tax on each crop fixed?
options: In grain only, taken by soldiers
By each zamindar alone, with no records
In cash, at a rate set for each crop
mughal-empire.explanation: After surveying the land and crops, the Mughals fixed a cash rate for each crop in each revenue circle.

mughal-empire.text: Meera draws a family tree for her project on the Mughals. She places four names from the earliest to the latest in time. Which order is correct?
mughal-empire.explanation: Genghis Khan came first, then Timur (who took Delhi in 1398), then Babur (1526) and then Akbar.

mughal-empire.text: Imran visits Panipat in Haryana. His guide says two great battles there decided who ruled north India, one in 1526 and one in 1556. Which pair is matched correctly?
mughal-empire.explanation: Babur won in 1526 against Ibrahim Lodi, and Akbar's side won in 1556 against Hemu.

mughal-empire.text: Zoya reads a museum card: 'Humayun, 1530 to 1540 and 1555 to 1556'. What explains the gap between 1540 and 1555?
options: He gave the throne to his son Akbar for fifteen years
He was held prisoner by Rana Sanga for fifteen years
He lost the throne to Sher Shah Suri and regained it in 1555
He went on a pilgrimage to Mecca for fifteen years
mughal-empire.explanation: Humayun was driven out by Sher Shah Suri after Chausa and Kanauj, and came back to Delhi in 1555.

mughal-empire.text: Meera is writing a project on how Akbar's empire was run. She needs details of the army, the officials and the revenue. Which source by Abu'l Fazl should she use?
mughal-empire.explanation: The Ain-i-Akbari describes Akbar's administration, including the army, officials and revenue.

mughal-empire.text: Rahim and Hari, one a Muslim and the other a Hindu, both apply for posts at Akbar's court. The officer is told to judge them only by their ability and not by their religion. Which idea of Akbar does this show?
mughal-empire.explanation: Sulh-i-kul, or universal peace, meant fair treatment of people of all religions.

mughal-empire.text: Hari reads that Akbar invited Muslim scholars, Brahmanas, Jesuit priests and Zoroastrians to discuss religion at the Ibadat Khana in Fatehpur Sikri. What does this show about Akbar?
options: He wanted every subject to give up his faith
He was interested in learning about many religions
He wanted to ban all religions except one
He wanted to collect taxes from priests
mughal-empire.explanation: The discussions in the Ibadat Khana show Akbar's curiosity about, and respect for, many faiths.

mughal-empire.text: Tanvi draws a family tree of the Mughals: Akbar, then a missing name, then Shah Jahan. Who fills the blank?
mughal-empire.explanation: Akbar's son Jahangir ruled from 1605 and was followed by his son Shah Jahan.

mughal-empire.text: Neha visits the Red Fort in Delhi. She learns that the walled city around it was built by an emperor and named after himself. What is the city called?
mughal-empire.explanation: Shah Jahan built the Red Fort and the city of Shahjahanabad in Delhi.

mughal-empire.text: When Shah Jahan fell ill, his sons fought each other for the throne. The winner put his father in prison. Which son won?
mughal-empire.explanation: Aurangzeb won the war of succession and became emperor in 1658.

mughal-empire.text: After an emperor died, two of his sons each claimed the throne, and a war followed. Which Mughal tradition made this likely?
options: Only the youngest son could ever rule
Every son had a claim to a share, as the Mughals did not follow primogeniture
The nobles picked the ruler by drawing lots
The throne always passed to the eldest son
mughal-empire.explanation: Since all sons could claim the inheritance, princes often fought to win the throne.

mughal-empire.text: Hasan is a mansabdar who must keep 300 horsemen ready for the emperor's army. Which term describes this number?
mughal-empire.explanation: Sawar is the number of horsemen a mansabdar had to maintain, while zat showed his personal rank.

mughal-empire.text: In Aurangzeb's last years, the number of mansabdars grew, but there were not enough good jagirs to give them. What was one result?
options: Zat ranks were abolished and all mansabdars were paid in grain
Peasants were freed from paying any revenue
The zabt system was introduced for the first time
Many mansabdars waited long for jagirs, and some jagirdars pressed peasants hard for more revenue
mughal-empire.explanation: With too few jagirs, mansabdars waited long and jagirdars tried to take as much revenue as possible from peasants.

mughal-empire.text: In Gopal's village, officials measured the land, noted crop yields and prices over many years, and fixed a cash revenue rate for each crop. What was this system called?
mughal-empire.explanation: The zabt system of Akbar and Todar Mal measured land and fixed cash rates for each crop.

mughal-empire.text: Kabir makes a timeline of Humayun's defeats. Humayun lost at Chausa in 1539. Where did he lose to Sher Khan in 1540?
mughal-empire.explanation: Sher Khan defeated Humayun at Chausa in 1539 and again at Kanauj in 1540.

mughal-empire.text: A Rajput ruler accepted Akbar's authority and joined the Mughal service. What position did the Mughals usually give such a ruler?
mughal-empire.explanation: Rajput rulers who joined Akbar were given ranks as mansabdars and served the empire.

mughal-empire.text: Zoya reads that in the 1700s the governors of Awadh, Bengal and Hyderabad began to rule almost like independent rulers. What does this show?
options: Akbar's mansabdari system had been revived
The Mughals had fully conquered the Deccan
Sher Shah's Sur dynasty had returned to power
The Mughal emperor's control over the provinces had weakened
mughal-empire.explanation: Provincial governors acted on their own because the emperors in Delhi were no longer strong enough to control them.

mughal-empire.text: Which of these is NOT linked with Akbar?
options: He built the Taj Mahal at Agra
Abu'l Fazl wrote about his reign
He promoted the idea of sulh-i-kul
He held discussions with scholars in the Ibadat Khana
mughal-empire.explanation: The Taj Mahal was built by Shah Jahan, not by Akbar.

mughal-empire.text: Which of these statements about Sher Shah Suri is NOT true?
options: He drove Humayun out of Delhi
He founded the Mughal Empire after the First Battle of Panipat
He belonged to the Sur dynasty
He issued a silver coin called the rupya
mughal-empire.explanation: The Mughal Empire was founded by Babur at Panipat in 1526; Sher Shah belonged to the rival Sur dynasty.

mughal-empire.text: Which of these is NOT true about mansabdars?
options: They were given a rank by the emperor
Their rank was shown by zat and sawar
They always lived on their jagirs and ruled them as local kings
Many were paid by receiving revenue from jagirs
mughal-empire.explanation: A mansabdar usually did not live on his jagir; his servants collected the revenue while he served elsewhere.

mughal-empire.text: Which of these is NOT true about Jahangir?
options: He was the son of Akbar
He was the son of Shah Jahan
mughal-empire.explanation: Jahangir was the father of Shah Jahan, not his son.

mughal-empire.text: Which of these is NOT true about Aurangzeb?
options: He came to the throne after a struggle among Shah Jahan's sons
He spent many years fighting in the Deccan
mughal-empire.explanation: Aurangzeb came after Jahangir and Shah Jahan, and was the sixth Mughal emperor in line.

mughal-empire.text: Which of these is NOT true of the Mughal empire in the 1700s?
options: Nadir Shah's invasion of 1739 weakened Delhi
Provincial governors became more obedient and sent larger revenues to Delhi
Powerful governors made their provinces nearly independent
Long wars in the Deccan had drained the treasury
mughal-empire.explanation: In the 1700s the Mughal empire weakened and governors often kept their revenues and power for themselves.

mughal-empire.text: Which of these statements about Mughal battles is NOT correct?
options: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526
Akbar's side defeated Hemu at Panipat in 1556
Aurangzeb won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526
Sher Khan defeated Humayun at Chausa in 1539
mughal-empire.explanation: The First Battle of Panipat in 1526 was won by Babur; Aurangzeb ruled much later.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): Babur is regarded as the founder of Mughal rule in India. Reason (R): In 1526 he defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: Babur's victory over Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 is exactly why he is called the founder of Mughal rule.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): Historians value the Akbarnama and the Ain-i-Akbari as sources on Akbar's reign. Reason (R): Abu'l Fazl, who wrote them, was a court historian who recorded the events and administration of the reign.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: Being written by Akbar's own court historian, these books record the reign in detail, which makes them valuable.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): Akbar's policy of sulh-i-kul was one of peace and tolerance towards all his subjects. Reason (R): Akbar introduced sulh-i-kul so that only one religion would be followed at his court.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: Sulh-i-kul meant universal peace, so the policy was tolerant; it was the opposite of allowing only one religion.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): Shah Jahan was a grandson of Akbar. Reason (R): Aurangzeb was a son of Shah Jahan.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: Shah Jahan was the son of Jahangir, who was Akbar's son, so A is true; R is also true but says nothing about how Shah Jahan was related to Akbar.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): Many Rajput rulers who accepted Akbar's authority were given high ranks in his service. Reason (R): Akbar wanted the support of the Rajput rulers to strengthen his empire.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: Akbar rewarded Rajput rulers with high ranks because he wished to gain their support.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): A mansabdar who held a jagir did not usually live on that land. Reason (R): A jagir gave only the right to collect revenue, which his servants collected while he served elsewhere.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: Since a jagir was only a revenue assignment, the mansabdar did not need to stay there.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): Humayun defeated Sher Khan at Chausa and ruled without a break until his death. Reason (R): Humayun regained his throne in 1555 after years away from Delhi.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: Humayun lost at Chausa and had to leave, so A is false; R is true as he returned in 1555.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): Aurangzeb's long wars in the Deccan put a heavy strain on the Mughal empire. Reason (R): The wars were very costly and kept the emperor and his army far from northern India for many years.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: The huge cost and long absence from the north are the reasons the wars strained the empire.

mughal-empire.text: Assertion (A): Zamindars were officers sent from the capital who had no local power. Reason (R): Zamindars helped collect revenue from peasants in the Mughal countryside.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
mughal-empire.explanation: Zamindars were local headmen and chiefs with real power in their areas, so A is false; R is true.

rulers-buildings.text: In post-and-lintel (trabeate) construction, a horizontal beam called a lintel is placed across two
rulers-buildings.explanation: A lintel rests on upright posts or columns, which is why the method is called post-and-lintel.

rulers-buildings.text: What is an arch?
options: A flat stone laid across two pillars
A rounded, hollow roof over a big hall
A curved structure over an opening that carries the weight above it to its sides
A tall tower built beside a mosque
rulers-buildings.explanation: An arch is a curve of stones over an opening that passes the load above it down to its supports at the sides.

rulers-buildings.text: The style of building that uses arches and domes is called
rulers-buildings.explanation: Arcuate construction is based on arches and domes, while trabeate construction uses beams across columns.

rulers-buildings.text: When lime mortar is mixed with stone chips and left to set hard, the material formed is called
rulers-buildings.explanation: Lime mortar mixed with stone chips sets into a hard mass called concrete, which builders used to make strong walls and domes.

rulers-buildings.text: A dome is
options: a rounded, hollow roof built over a building
a horizontal beam across two pillars
a straight flight of stone steps
a wall built around a garden
rulers-buildings.explanation: A dome is a rounded roof that is hollow inside and covers a hall or a tomb.

rulers-buildings.text: Meena visits an old temple. Its doorway has two upright stone pillars with one flat stone laid across the top. Which building method was used for this doorway?
rulers-buildings.explanation: Two upright supports with a horizontal stone across them is the post-and-lintel, or trabeate, method.

rulers-buildings.text: Farhan builds a model gateway. A flat beam over a wide gap breaks, but a curved arch of blocks over the same gap stands firm. What best explains this?
options: The arch passes the weight above it to its sides and supports, so it can cover a wider opening
The arch removes all the weight from the wall
The flat beam was too short to touch the ground
rulers-buildings.explanation: In an arch the load is carried along the curve to the supports, so wider openings become possible.

rulers-buildings.text: Assertion (A): Arches helped builders make wide doorways and large halls. Reason (R): In an arch the weight of the structure above is carried by the curve to the supports at its sides.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
rulers-buildings.explanation: The curve carries the load sideways to the supports, and that is exactly why wide openings became possible.

rulers-buildings.text: Which of these is NOT a feature of arcuate construction?
options: A single flat beam carrying all the weight above an opening
rulers-buildings.explanation: Carrying the weight on a flat beam is trabeate construction. Arcuate buildings use arches, domes and vaults.

rulers-buildings.text: The Rajarajeshvara temple at Thanjavur is dedicated to which god?
rulers-buildings.explanation: The Rajarajeshvara temple is a Shiva temple, and its name joins the king's name with the god's title.

rulers-buildings.text: Which ruler built the Rajarajeshvara temple at Thanjavur?
rulers-buildings.explanation: Rajaraja Chola built it and gave it a name that joined his own name with Ishvara, the Lord. His son Rajendra built another capital and temple at Gangaikondacholapuram.

rulers-buildings.text: Ilango reads that Rajendra I, son of Rajaraja Chola, built a new capital city with a grand temple. Which place is this?
rulers-buildings.explanation: Rajendra Chola built the city and temple of Gangaikondacholapuram. Thanjavur is the town of his father's Rajarajeshvara temple.

rulers-buildings.text: Lakshmi from Chennai visits a huge Chola temple at Thanjavur, and her teacher says it shows the power of the king who built it. Which temple is she visiting?
rulers-buildings.explanation: The great Chola temple at Thanjavur is the Rajarajeshvara temple, built by Rajaraja Chola.

rulers-buildings.text: Sunita notices that King Rajaraja gave his own name to the temple, calling it Rajarajeshvara. What does this best show?
options: The temple was built by traders
Only priests were allowed to enter
The temple was built after his death by a foreign ruler
The king wanted to link his name and power with the god and be remembered
rulers-buildings.explanation: Rulers used grand temples to show their devotion and power, and putting the king's own name on the temple tied his fame to the god.

rulers-buildings.text: Assertion (A): Rulers like the Chola kings built very large temples. Reason (R): A grand temple showed the ruler's power and wealth as well as his devotion.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
rulers-buildings.explanation: Big temples were a way to display a king's strength and riches along with his faith, so R explains A.

rulers-buildings.text: Which of these is NOT true of the Rajarajeshvara temple?
options: It was built by Akbar to mark his victory in Gujarat
It was built by Rajaraja Chola
Its name joins the king's name with the title of the god
rulers-buildings.explanation: Akbar built the Buland Darwaza for his victory in Gujarat. The Rajarajeshvara temple is a Chola work.

rulers-buildings.text: Which Sultan completed the Qutb Minar that Qutbuddin Aybak had begun?
rulers-buildings.explanation: Qutbuddin Aybak began the Qutb Minar and Iltutmish completed it.

rulers-buildings.text: The Alai Darwaza was built by
rulers-buildings.explanation: The Alai Darwaza, a gateway with arches, was built by Alauddin Khalji and is named after him.

rulers-buildings.text: Quwwat-ul-Islam is the name of a
options: mosque in the Qutb complex in Delhi
rulers-buildings.explanation: Quwwat-ul-Islam is the mosque standing near the Qutb Minar in Delhi.

rulers-buildings.text: Zoya visits the Qutb complex in Delhi. She sees a tall minar, a mosque beside it and a gateway with arches. Which pair names the mosque and the gateway?
rulers-buildings.explanation: The mosque in the Qutb complex is Quwwat-ul-Islam and its gateway is the Alai Darwaza. The Buland Darwaza is at Fatehpur Sikri.

rulers-buildings.text: Assertion (A): The Qutb Minar stands in Delhi. Reason (R): Iltutmish helped to complete the Qutb Minar.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
rulers-buildings.explanation: Both statements are true, but finishing the minar does not explain why it stands in Delhi.

rulers-buildings.text: Which of these is NOT part of the Qutb complex in Delhi?
rulers-buildings.explanation: The Buland Darwaza is at Fatehpur Sikri, built by Akbar.

rulers-buildings.text: Which Sultan built the fortified city of Tughluqabad near Delhi?
rulers-buildings.explanation: Tughluqabad was founded by Ghiyasuddin Tughluq and carries the name of his dynasty.

rulers-buildings.text: Arjun's teacher writes four monuments on the board: Qutb Minar, Alai Darwaza, Tughluqabad and Taj Mahal. Which one was built last?
rulers-buildings.explanation: The first three belong to the Delhi Sultanate. The Taj Mahal was built much later by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

rulers-buildings.text: Hina visits the ruins of Tughluqabad near Delhi and says it was a fort-city of the Mughals. Her father corrects her. Whose city was it?
options: The Delhi Sultans of the Tughluq dynasty
rulers-buildings.explanation: Tughluqabad was built by the Tughluq Sultans of Delhi, long before the Mughals.

rulers-buildings.text: Sher Shah Suri's tomb stands at
rulers-buildings.explanation: Sher Shah's tomb is at Sasaram in Bihar.

rulers-buildings.text: Humayun's tomb stands in which city?
rulers-buildings.explanation: Humayun's tomb, a Mughal tomb set in a garden, is in Delhi.

rulers-buildings.text: Priya visits a Mughal tomb in Delhi. It has a big dome and arched openings, and the garden around it is divided into four parts by walkways and water channels. Which building is it?
rulers-buildings.explanation: Humayun's tomb in Delhi stands in a charbagh garden. Sher Shah's tomb is at Sasaram and the Taj Mahal is at Agra.

rulers-buildings.text: Assertion (A): Sher Shah's tomb was built by Shah Jahan. Reason (R): Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
rulers-buildings.explanation: Sher Shah's tomb at Sasaram was built for Sher Shah Suri, not by Shah Jahan, so A is false. R is a true fact.

rulers-buildings.text: The Buland Darwaza is at
rulers-buildings.explanation: The Buland Darwaza is the tall gateway at Fatehpur Sikri near Agra.

rulers-buildings.text: The Buland Darwaza was built to celebrate Akbar's victory over
rulers-buildings.explanation: Akbar built the Buland Darwaza after his victory in Gujarat.
